To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children prefer speakers who are not only accurate, but also sufficient in providing information.
preschool-age children prefer speakers who give sufficient information, whereas school-age children also prefer speakers who give good quality information.
Preschoolers and school-age children prefer speakers who give sufficient information over speakers who give insufficient information, but only when the outcome of that information is clear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how children learn to evaluate the information provided by others.
the question how children learn about others' preferences, and what information children rely on to establish these preferences.
the development of social cognition in preschoolers and school-aged children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
preschoolers are not able to make use of information quality when the outcome of that information is ambiguous, whereas school-age children are.
preschoolers prefer sufficient information, whereas older children prefer sufficient over insufficient information.
children use information quality as a speaker preference cue, but that the use of information quality is not fully established at preschool age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children's use of speaker preferences to select informants is influenced by their understanding of information quality and that this influence increases with development.
children use information quality as a basis to establish speaker preferences, but that this use is more effective when children can evaluate the outcome of a speaker's clue.
preschoolers do not use information quality to determine that a speaker is a better informant, whereas school-aged children do.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children can use information quality to establish preferences for speakers.
children can use information quality to make inferences about the speaker's competence and, in the case of older children, to make decisions about whom to solicit further information.
young children's use of speaker quality as a cue for establishing speaker preferences is a developmental phenomenon.
